title: Hear, O Israel: Love the LORD with Everything
summary: Moses gives the heart of the whole law: the LORD is one, and Israel must love him with all their heart, soul, and strength. These words are to be taught to children, spoken of through every part of the day, and marked on hands, foreheads, doorposts, and gates. He warns that prosperity in the new land will tempt Israel to forget the God who freed them, and he tells parents how to answer when a child asks what the commandments mean.
story: In chapter 5 Moses repeated the Ten Commandments and recalled how the people begged him to hear the rest of God's words for them. Chapter 6 begins to deliver those words, and it starts not with a rule about sacrifice or property but with love. Chapters 6 to 11 are an extended appeal to loyalty before the detailed laws of chapters 12 to 26, and this chapter sets the tone for everything after it. The people are about to move from a wilderness where they depended on God for daily bread into a land of cities and vineyards they did not build. Moses knows that abundance can do what hunger could not: make them forget.
historical:
The setting is still the plains of Moab before the crossing of the Jordan (see the note on Deuteronomy 5 for the book's date and its treaty form). Ancient treaties required a subject people to love their overlord, meaning to be loyal to him alone, and to teach that loyalty to their descendants; Assyrian loyalty oaths of the seventh century BC use this language. Deuteronomy takes the political vocabulary of loyalty and applies it to Israel's relationship with God, though the chapter's warmth goes beyond anything in those treaties.

The chapter's later life is well documented. Small leather cases holding handwritten passages of the law, called tefillin or phylacteries, were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls at Qumran, showing that by about the first century BC some Jews were fulfilling verse 8 literally. The Nash Papyrus, a small Hebrew fragment from Egypt usually dated to the second or first century BC, contains the Ten Commandments followed by the Shema, which suggests the two were read together in worship. The Mishnah, the collection of Jewish law compiled around AD 200, opens with rules for reciting the Shema morning and evening, a practice observant Jews keep today.
cultural:
The word Shema, Hebrew for hear, gives this confession its name. In Hebrew, to hear is also to heed; the same verb covers listening and obeying. The body language of the chapter would have made sense to a first reader. The heart, in Hebrew thought, is not mainly the seat of feeling but of thinking, choosing, and purpose. The soul (nephesh) is the whole living self, one's very life. The third term, usually translated strength, is the ordinary Hebrew word for very or much, used here as a noun: love God with all your muchness, everything you have. The three together mean the whole person, inside and out.

Verses 7 to 9 cover every place and time in an ancient household: sitting at home and walking on the road, lying down and getting up, the hand that works and the forehead that thinks, the doorpost of the house and the gate of the town, where elders met and justice was done. Jewish tradition came to observe verses 8 and 9 literally with tefillin and the mezuzah (a small case fixed to the doorpost). Others have read the verses as a vivid figure for keeping God's words constantly before one's mind and deeds. Both readings agree that faith was meant to fill ordinary life, not stay in a sanctuary.
literary: The chapter is a sermon built around a single confession. Verses 1 to 3 introduce it with a call to hear and obey. Verses 4 and 5 state the confession and command, six Hebrew words for the first and a threefold totality for the second. Verses 6 to 9 then spread the command outward from the heart to the home, the road, the body, and the town. Verses 10 to 19 turn to warning, with a striking series of negatives: cities you did not build, houses you did not fill, wells you did not dig, vineyards you did not plant. The chapter closes with a catechism, a question a child asks and the answer a parent gives (verses 20 to 25), which retells the exodus in the first person plural: “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt.”

outline.t: Keep the commands so that you may live and prosper
The Shema: the LORD is one; love him with all you are
Do not forget the LORD in the land of plenty
When your son asks: the story behind the commands

doctrines.note: The Shema confesses that Israel's God is one: not one god among many, but the only LORD, owed undivided loyalty. The Christian doctrine of the Trinity does not set this aside; the church has always confessed one God, and the New Testament writers, all of them Jews, affirmed the Shema while confessing Jesus as Lord.

The law's first demand is love, not mere compliance. Every other command in Deuteronomy is an expression of this one, and Jesus names it the first and greatest commandment. Obedience that is not rooted in love has missed the point.

Faith is to be passed on in the home, through daily conversation and honest answers to children's questions. The chapter gives parents a script that begins with the story of rescue before it gets to rules.

The danger Moses fears is not hardship but comfort. When Israel eats and is satisfied, they may forget the God who brought them out of slavery and follow the gods of the peoples around them. Prosperity is named as a spiritual threat.

words.note: Shama, to hear. In Hebrew the word runs from hearing a sound to listening closely to obeying, and it often means all three at once. The call “Hear, O Israel” (verses 3 and 4) is therefore a summons to attention and to obedience together. It gives the Shema its name.

Echad, one. The same word describes the man and woman becoming one flesh (Genesis 2:24), so it can describe a unity that is not bare singleness. Verse 4 can be translated “the LORD is one” or “the LORD alone,” and scholars debate whether the emphasis falls on God's uniqueness, his unity, or Israel's exclusive loyalty. The readings overlap, and all rule out other gods.

Ahav, to love. In treaties, love meant loyal allegiance. Here it includes that loyalty but goes further, since Deuteronomy also speaks of God's own love for Israel's fathers (4:37, 7:8). Israel's love for God answers his love for them. It is commanded, which shows that biblical love is a settled commitment and not only a feeling.

Me'od, very, much, exceedingly. Usually an adverb, here it is used as a noun and translated strength. It means the full measure of one's capacity and resources. Later Jewish interpreters sometimes took it to include one's possessions, a reading that fits the chapter's concern with wealth.

christ: When Jesus was asked which commandment is the most important, he answered with this chapter: “Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is One” and the command to love God with all one's heart, soul, mind, and strength, joined to the command to love one's neighbor (Mark 12:29-31). When the devil tempted him in the wilderness, Jesus answered from this same chapter, refusing to put God to the test (verse 16, quoted in Matthew 4:7) and insisting on worshiping and serving God only (verse 13, in Luke 4:8 and Matthew 4:10). Where Israel tested God at Massah, Jesus kept faith in the wilderness. Paul, writing to Corinth, reworks the Shema's words, speaking of one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 8:6). Many scholars read that verse as placing Jesus within the identity of the one God Israel confessed, which is how the church came to confess the Trinity without abandoning the Shema.

hard.q: Verse 25 says keeping the commands will be Israel's righteousness. Does that mean salvation is earned by obedience?
hard.a: Read on its own, verse 25 can sound like a formula for earning God's favor. But the answer the parent gives begins with rescue, not effort: “We were slaves of Pharaoh in Egypt, but the LORD brought us out” (verse 21). God's saving act comes first, and obedience is the response of a people already redeemed. The word righteousness here refers to living rightly within a covenant God has already made, being in right standing as his faithful people, rather than to earning a place in it. Jewish interpreters have long read the law this way, as a gracious gift to a chosen people. Christian readers differ in how they relate this verse to Paul's teaching that no one is justified by works of the law (for example Romans 3:20 and Galatians 2:16). Some see Deuteronomy describing the covenant life of those already saved; others see the verse as holding out a standard that sinful people cannot finally meet, which the New Testament says Christ met on their behalf. Both readings agree that in Deuteronomy grace comes before obedience, not after it.

questions: Loving God with heart, soul, and strength means the whole person. Which part of your life do you find hardest to include in that love?
Moses feared that comfort would make Israel forget God. Where has plenty, rather than hardship, made you less aware of your need for him?
The chapter pictures faith passed on in ordinary conversation at home and on the road. What would it look like to talk about God naturally in the everyday rhythms of your household or friendships?
